conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m Dr. Lee, one of your hospital doctors. You’re here because of severe muscle weakness. Can you tell me more about what’s been going on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I’ve been feeling weaker every day for about a week. I usually walk around my house, but now I can barely stand without holding onto something.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That sounds really tough. Does this feel like any of your past flare-ups with polymyositis?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Exactly like them. I’ve been in remission for years, but this feels just like before—my arms and legs are so weak.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. Your blood test from the clinic showed a very high muscle enzyme level—CK was 2550. That confirms this is likely a flare of your polymyositis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, that’s high. I didn’t feel much better after the steroid shot in the ER.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It takes time. We’re starting you on strong IV steroids for three days to calm the inflammation. You may not feel better right away.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I also feel a bit short of breath. Not terrible—maybe a 3 out of 10—but it’s there.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we noticed some fluid overload. You got a diuretic in the ER and passed over 5 liters of urine. Your lungs have mild congestion, but no pneumonia.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. I’ve had heart failure flares before. I used to take torsemide, but I stopped months ago because of my job.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We understand. For now, we’re monitoring you closely. You’re on CPAP at night, which helps with breathing and heart strain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. And I haven’t been taking my warfarin the past few days because I was so weak and couldn’t get to the pharmacy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your INR was low at 1.4, so we restarted warfarin. We’re not using IV heparin to bridge, but your clinic will watch your levels closely after discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll make sure to follow up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your labs from this morning show your CK is coming down—from 2500 to 955. That’s a good sign the steroids are working.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great! Do you think I’ll be able to walk better soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It will take time. We’re transitioning you from IV steroids to oral prednisone—60 mg daily. You’ll stay on that for a while.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I remember prednisone makes my blood sugar go up. I have diabetes too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. We’ve been managing your sugars with insulin in the hospital. But since you prefer not to use insulin at home, we’re adding metformin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I can take that. But will it be enough with the steroids?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re restarting your glipizide and liraglutide too. Metformin will help extra. Your PCP can adjust doses later if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That sounds good. My blood pressure has been high too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s been up to 190s over 120s. Steroids can make that worse. We’re keeping your metoprolol and increasing losartan from 25 to 50 mg daily.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll keep an eye on it at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The rheumatology team met with you earlier. They’re restarting mycophenolate—Cellcept—twice a day to help control your polymyositis long-term.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I took that before. Is Rituximab also coming back?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: They’re considering it. You’ll discuss that with your rheumatologist at your follow-up. For now, we’re focused on getting the flare under control.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Makes sense. Will I need to take antibiotics too?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’re starting Bactrim—one tablet daily—to prevent a lung infection called PJP, which can happen with high-dose steroids.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I remember that. I used to take it three times a week, but daily is easier to remember.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. Your breathing is better, your heart function is stable, and your weakness is slowly improving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I can lift my arms better. But I still need help standing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s expected. We’ll keep working on it. Your discharge is planned for tomorrow morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. What will my meds be at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll take prednisone 60 mg daily, mycophenolate twice a day, Bactrim daily, and your usual diabetes meds plus new metformin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my blood pressure med is now 50 mg losartan?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. And warfarin every day. Please follow up with your clinic to check your INR—it was still low this morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. I’ll also see my rheumatologist soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, to plan your steroid taper and discuss Rituximab. We’ll send all the details to your doctors.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re cleared to go home. Keep using your BiPAP at night, take all your medications, and call if you feel worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I feel much more stable than when I came in.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. We’re glad the treatment helped. Rest, follow up, and take care.
